candidate.blueprint_locator: Health Promotion and Maintenance client-needs subcategory (6–12% of items), within Health Promotion and Maintenance; this item tests evidence-based risk-reduction counseling and client education for tobacco cessation.
candidate.blueprint_topic: Health-promotion counseling and evidence-based tobacco-cessation support
candidate.educational_objective: Teach nonpregnant adults who smoke that combining behavioral counseling with appropriate cessation pharmacotherapy provides the strongest evidence-based support for quitting, with follow-up and repeated support as needed.

options.A: Using behavioral counseling together with an appropriate quit-smoking medication offers the best chance of successful cessation
options.B: Medication should be avoided because counseling and approved cessation medications are ineffective when used together
options.C: A single brief conversation is always sufficient, so follow-up support is unnecessary
options.D: Evidence-based cessation treatment is useful only after smoking-related lung disease has already developed

candidate.rationale: A is correct. Current CDC guidance states that counseling and medication are each effective for adults who smoke, and using them together provides the best chance of quitting successfully. CDC clinical guidance also recommends offering a combination of counseling and medications and providing follow-up support because quitting may require multiple attempts. B contradicts the evidence for combined treatment. C incorrectly converts brief advice into a universally sufficient intervention and ignores ongoing support. D is incorrect because cessation benefits health regardless of whether smoking-related lung disease has already developed. The stem specifies a nonpregnant adult because medication decisions during pregnancy require separate individualized risk-benefit consideration.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Current CDC guidance directly supports combined behavioral counseling and cessation medication for nonpregnant adults who smoke and supports continuing follow-up rather than assuming one encounter is universally sufficient.
candidate.source_document_title: How to Quit Smoking; Clinical Interventions to Treat Tobacco Use and Dependence Among Adults
candidate.source_locator: CDC 'How to Quit Smoking' → 'Counseling plus medications': using counseling and medication together gives people who smoke the best chance of quitting for good. CDC 'Clinical Interventions to Treat Tobacco Use and Dependence Among Adults' → 'Combining treatments': counseling and medication are effective alone but are more effective together; 'Offer patients treatment': offer a combination of counseling and medications; 'Follow up with patients': assess progress over time and provide additional support because multiple attempts may be needed. Pregnancy section separately advises behavioral interventions first and individualized medication decisions.
candidate.source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
candidate.source_version_date: CDC pages dated 2024-05-15 and 2024-05-14 and current at access 2026-08-18
candidate.stem: A nonpregnant adult client who smokes cigarettes wants to quit. Which nursing teaching is most consistent with current CDC guidance?
